description: We are QuemandoTokens, a team focused on AI and software development. We work with Python, JavaScript, APIs and LLMs, turning ideas into working prototypes quickly. We are looking for people with skills in frontend, UI/UX, backend, data/AI or pitching who want to build a strong and polished project.
summary:
SITE REGRET is an interactive web application for comparing lunar landing-site conditions—and checking whether a preferred site remains preferable when assumptions change. Built for the Lunar Landing Site Navigator challenge, it combines NASA LRO/LOLA topography with NASA/JPL SPICE geometry to visualize the Sun and Earth relative to the terrain horizon.

Our prototype compares two Connecting Ridge locations across two 30-day windows, multiple observer heights, and alternative terrain surfaces. Users choose a criterion, compare results, inspect visibility timelines, and export findings with provenance.

One example shows why assumptions matter: at ground level in our December–January window, Site B has a shorter longest interval without Sun-center visibility than Site A: 14 h 40 min versus 38 h 40 min. Under one team-defined terrain hypothesis, the ranking reverses; keeping B adds 16 h 30 min to that interval. A different objective—maximizing Earth visibility—also changes the nominal winner.

SITE REGRET makes these trade-offs accessible for preliminary exploration and education. It reports geometric visibility, model sensitivity, and explicit limitations; it does not predict mission survival or certify a landing site.
details:
Project demo: start here

Watch our short submission demo — Two Moon Landing Sites. Which One Would You Choose?

Our under-30-second presentation introduces SITE REGRET and its central question: does a preferred lunar landing site remain preferable when terrain assumptions change? Then explore the live application and the evidence below. Longer explanatory videos are grouped separately under “Video learning guide”.

Figure 1. SITE REGRET Dashboard: an interactive lunar globe introduces the two Connecting Ridge locations and the guided mission. The globe provides geographic context; the composition is illustrative and is not a site-level visibility calculation.

A landing-site choice is only as useful as the assumptions behind it

Near the lunar south pole, the Sun stays close to the horizon. Local relief can block sunlight or the view of Earth, and changes in date, observer height, or terrain representation can change the comparison between candidate locations.

SITE REGRET brings these relationships into one interactive application. It addresses the Lunar Landing Site Navigator challenge by helping users compare sites and time windows, visualize Sun and Earth positions relative to the terrain horizon, and investigate why a preferred location can change.

Our primary use case is preliminary scenario exploration: a user compares alternatives and communicates the assumptions behind a result. The same guided experience helps educators, students, and the public understand lunar planning constraints.

Figure 2. Connecting Ridge sites A (ROI 4) and B (ROI 6), approximately 648 m apart. Background: NASA/JPL Moon Trek, LRO/LROC NAC mosaic (NASA/GSFC/Arizona State University). Mosaic shadows belong to the original image acquisitions, not the selected simulation time.

Start with a criterion, then compare

There is no single “best” site independently of the objective.

For the reference terrain in window W2—14 December 2026 to 13 January 2027 UTC—at ground level:

  • Site A · Connecting Ridge ROI 4: longest interval without Sun-center visibility: 38 h 40 min; total time with Earth-center visibility: 377 h 50 min.
  • Site B · Connecting Ridge ROI 6: longest interval without Sun-center visibility: 14 h 40 min; total time with Earth-center visibility: 371 h 50 min.

Site B wins when minimizing the longest interval without Sun-center visibility. Site A wins when maximizing total Earth visibility.

The application therefore asks users to select a criterion before revealing a winner. Its four criteria cover the longest interval without Sun visibility, total Sun visibility, total Earth visibility, and simultaneous Sun–Earth visibility.

Figure 3. Sun–Earth geometry and local sky at Site A, W2, 0 m, nominal terrain. At 14 December 2026 00:00 UTC, the Sun center is above the terrain horizon and the Earth center is below it. Geometry: NASA/JPL SPICE DE421; terrain: NASA LRO/LOLA. The orbital sketch is not to scale.

What happens when the terrain assumption changes?

In the same W2 ground-level case, the team-defined correlated_plus terrain hypothesis reverses the solar ranking:

  • Site A: 32 h 30 min without Sun-center visibility.
  • Site B: 49 h.
  • Keeping the reference choice, B, adds 16 h 30 min compared with choosing A under that hypothesis.

We call this difference decision regret: the loss, measured in the selected criterion, from keeping a choice when another performs better under a particular scenario. It is not a probability of failure.

Figure 4. W2, 0 m, criterion: minimize the longest interval without Sun-center visibility. The nominal terrain favors B; correlated_plus favors A, with 16 h 30 min regret for keeping B. Team hypotheses and published clones are displayed separately; their counts are not probabilities.

The published terrain realizations also produce different outcomes. In clone 0001, the computed intervals are 191 h 20 min at A and the full 720-hour window at B, giving a difference of 528 h 40 min. That full-window result is bounded by the evaluated period; it does not establish when visibility would return outside it.

These results motivate inspecting assumptions rather than treating one ranking as universal. The four team-defined hypotheses and five published clones remain separate throughout the application. They use different observer-height conventions, and their counts are not combined into probabilities or confidence levels.

Explore the result and its explanation

A complete user journey is:

  1. Select a time window and observer height.
  2. Choose a comparison criterion.
  3. Compare A and B.
  4. Inspect the Sun–Earth timeline and local horizon.
  5. Select an alternative terrain surface.
  6. Export the comparison with its selection and provenance.

The application provides complementary views:

  • Explore: georeferenced Moon Trek imagery, numeric LOLA elevation and quality layers, and access to PDS/ODE product information and footprints.
  • Timeline: Sun and Earth positions, terrain horizons, visibility states, and nominal rise/set intervals in UTC.
  • Compare: side-by-side metrics, criterion-dependent winners, and JSON/CSV exports.
  • Engineer: terrain, sightlines, and observer-height sensitivity. A separate nominal-terrain calculation covers 0–30 m at 0.5 m steps; alternative surfaces retain the core heights of 0, 2, and 10 m.
  • Regret Lab: which choices hold, tie, or reverse across the evaluated surfaces.
  • Evidence: source records, methodology, stored checks, convergence results, hashes, and limitations.

Engineer: see how height changes the horizon

Move from the map to a 3D view of the observer and terrain, then inspect how geometric visibility changes with height. The nominal-terrain package computes 61 observer heights from 0 to 30 m; alternative surfaces retain the core heights of 0, 2, and 10 m.

Figure 5. Engineer Mode, Site A, W2, nominal terrain, observer at 10 m (14 December 2026, 00:00 UTC). The 3D view and map connect the observer, solar viewing direction, and terrain setting the horizon. Elevation is derived from NASA LOLA; the tower and surface styling are illustrative. No structural feasibility or landing safety is inferred.

Figure 6. Engineer height analysis for Site A in W2 on nominal terrain. At 10 m, the computed window contains 720 h of Sun-center visibility, 399 h of Earth-center visibility, and no interval without Sun-center visibility. Curves show the nominal calculations from 0 to 30 m at 0.5 m steps. These are geometric results within the selected window, not power or radio-link performance.

NASA data drives the calculation

  • NASA Goddard PGDA 78 · LRO/LOLA Site01: local 5 m terrain, quality layers, regions of interest, and published terrain clones.
  • NASA Goddard PGDA 90: regional and distant terrain at 80 m and 240 m resolution.
  • NASA/JPL NAIF SPICE · DE421: Sun and Earth directions in the lunar reference frame.
  • NASA/JPL Horizons: sampled cross-check of apparent-position calculations.
  • NASA/JPL Moon Trek: published orbital image mosaics for geographic context.
  • NASA PDS Geosciences Node · ODE: product metadata and footprints.

A Python engine computes terrain horizons with lunar curvature and Sun/Earth geometry. The core package contains 120 precomputed scenarios: two sites × two windows × three heights × ten surfaces. The browser presents these results and verifies scientific data files against their recorded SHA-256 hashes.

The web application uses Next.js, React, TypeScript, OpenLayers, and Three.js.

Our contribution

Existing NASA tools and published research provide the essential mapping, ephemerides, terrain, and uncertainty methods. SITE REGRET builds on that foundation with a decision-focused experience: choose an objective, compare outcomes, challenge the terrain assumption, and inspect the consequence of keeping a choice.

Our contribution is the integration and communication of that reasoning through an accessible, traceable interface. We do not claim to have invented terrain-uncertainty analysis.

Evidence and interpretation

The scientific package records 414 internal checks, including analytic geometry and sampling-convergence checks. Eight JPL Horizons comparisons examine agreement between apparent-position calculations at sampled times; the visibility calculation itself uses geometric DE421 directions.

These checks support specific parts of the computation. File hashes establish integrity, and interface tests check faithful presentation. Neither constitutes independent certification of terrain accuracy or operational readiness.

The prototype covers two fixed locations approximately 648 m apart and two development windows, rather than arbitrary coordinates or mission dates. Both locations have interpolated heights according to the LOLA return-count layer.

Visibility means the geometric center of the Sun or Earth is above the modeled terrain horizon. Core time metrics use 10-minute intervals, and continuous intervals are clipped to the selected window.

The team’s terrain perturbations are sensitivity experiments, not calibrated NASA error estimates. Only five of the provider’s 100 published clones are evaluated; they do not establish the behavior of the complete ensemble.

Geometric visibility informs further analysis. It does not calculate solar-array output, battery endurance, thermal survival, radio-link performance, or landing safety. Our intended impact is clearer preliminary comparison and scientific understanding; operational benefit and usability still require external evaluation.

AI assistance and team responsibility

Claude Code assisted software development, testing, and documentation. Codex assisted research and submission editing. The scientific results are derived through the documented Python pipeline from published terrain data and deterministic geometry. Tool-specific contributions and review status are recorded in the repository.

The linked video materials include AI-generated content used to present and explain the project. Scientific claims, numerical results, assumptions, and limitations should be assessed through the documented data package and the Evidence view.

Video learning guide

For a deeper explanation, follow these supplementary videos from introductory context to decision sensitivity. These longer videos support the project description; the short submission demo is linked separately above and in the Project Demonstration field.

  1. The Sun Is Right There… So Why Is This Moon Site in Darkness? — 1 min 35 sec. Start with the question of terrain and lunar shadows.
  2. Can a Moon Landing Site See BOTH the Sun and Earth? — approximately 4 min. Continue with the two visibility objectives addressed by the challenge.
  3. We Changed the Terrain Model. Our Moon Landing Pick FLIPPED. — 8 min 6 sec. Explore the central comparison and how changing the terrain model can reverse a preferred choice.

Browse the Quemando Tokens YouTube channel for the presentation and explanatory videos. For exact definitions, numerical assumptions, sources, and limitations, consult the written methodology and the Evidence view.

Try SITE REGRET

  • Open the application in English
  • Inspect the W2 comparison and terrain sensitivity
  • Explore scientific evidence, sources, and limitations
  • Inspect source code and validation records

SITE REGRET is a prototype developed by team QuemandoTokens for NASA Space Apps Challenge Bilbao 2026. Its derived results are team outputs using NASA resources and do not imply NASA endorsement.
